title: Project: Autonomous Research Agent
summary: In this capstone-style project lesson, you build an autonomous research agent that takes a topic, plans a research strategy, calls web search and page-reading tools, synthesizes findings across sources, and produces a structured, citation-backed report. You'll design the agent loop, define tool schemas, add guardrails for cost and reliability, and validate output structure.
objectives: Design an agent loop (plan → act → observe → synthesize) for autonomous research
Define and register web tools (search and fetch) with clear JSON schemas
Implement source synthesis that aggregates and deduplicates findings with citations
Generate a structured report using a validated output schema
Add guardrails for iteration limits, cost control, and error handling
Evaluate the agent's output for accuracy, coverage, and citation quality

quiz.q: What distinguishes an agent from a single LLM call?
options: It iterates through a plan-act-observe loop using tools
quiz.why: An agent's defining feature is the iterative loop where it reasons, calls tools, observes results, and decides next steps — unlike a one-shot LLM call.

quiz.q: Why do tools require a JSON parameter schema?
options: So the model knows how to invoke them correctly
quiz.why: The schema and description tell the model what arguments the tool expects and how to call it properly.

quiz.q: Which is the best practice for the final research report?
options: A validated schema where claims map to source URLs
quiz.why: A validated structured schema ensures every claim is traceable to a source and that downstream code can parse the output reliably.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an iteration cap (max_iters) in the agent loop?
options: To prevent infinite loops and runaway cost
To increase the number of sources
quiz.why: An iteration cap is a guardrail that stops the loop from running indefinitely, controlling both reliability and cost.

quiz.q: In one sentence, name the five stages of the ReAct-style research loop.
quiz.answer: Plan, Act, Observe, Repeat (until stopping), and Synthesize.
quiz.why: The agent plans research questions, acts by calling a tool, observes the result, repeats until a stopping condition, then synthesizes the report.

quiz.q: Short answer: Give one reason citation quality is critical when evaluating the agent.
quiz.answer: It lets you verify claims are actually supported by real, relevant sources (accuracy and trustworthiness).
quiz.why: Citations make the report verifiable; without accurate, relevant sources the findings can't be trusted or fact-checked.

slides.title: Project: Autonomous Research Agent
slides.narration: Welcome to the capstone project for this module. We're going to build an autonomous research agent: a system that takes a topic, decides what to look up, uses web tools to gather evidence, and produces a structured, citation-backed report. By the end you'll understand the full agent loop and how to ship it reliably.

slides.title: What Makes It an Agent
bullets: More than a single LLM call — it iterates
Plans research questions, then acts
Calls external tools and observes results
Decides its own next steps until done
slides.narration: The difference between a chatbot and an agent is the loop. A single LLM call just answers from what it already knows. An agent plans, takes actions in the world through tools, observes the results, and then decides what to do next. That autonomy is what lets it research a topic it has never seen specific data on.

slides.title: The ReAct Loop
bullets: Plan: break topic into sub-questions
Act: call a tool like web_search
Observe: read and store the result
Repeat until a stopping condition
Synthesize the final report
slides.narration: The core pattern is ReAct, short for Reason and Act. The agent reasons about what it needs, takes an action by calling a tool, observes the output, and repeats. We keep a scratchpad of the running conversation so the model can reason over everything it has found so far. When it has enough, it stops and synthesizes.

slides.title: Defining Tools
bullets: Each tool: name, description, JSON schema
web_search returns titles, URLs, snippets
fetch_page returns cleaned page text
Schema teaches the model how to call it
slides.narration: Tools are functions the model can invoke. Each one needs a clear name, a description, and a JSON parameter schema. The description and schema are how the model learns what the tool does and how to call it correctly. For research we need at least two: web_search to find sources, and fetch_page to read them in full.

slides.title: The Orchestration Loop
bullets: Send messages + tools to the model
If it returns tool_calls, run them
Append results back as tool messages
Loop until no tool calls or max_iters
slides.narration: Here's the orchestration in code. We send the message history and available tools to the model. If the model responds with tool calls, we execute each one, append the results back into the message list, and loop again. When the model stops requesting tools, it's signalling that it's ready to write the report.

slides.title: Structured Output
bullets: Define a report schema up front
Key findings map to source URLs
Use JSON mode + validate with Pydantic
Downstream code can rely on the shape
slides.narration: Never let the final report be free-form text. Define a schema with a summary, key findings each tied to source URLs, open questions, and a source list. Use the model's structured output mode and validate the result with something like Pydantic. This guarantees every claim is traceable to a source and that downstream systems can parse it reliably.

slides.title: Guardrails
bullets: Iteration cap to prevent infinite loops
Budget cap on tokens and tool calls
Try/except around tools, return errors to model
Deduplicate URLs; enforce fetch timeouts
slides.narration: Autonomous loops can misbehave, so guardrails are essential. Always cap iterations and track a spending budget. Wrap tool calls in error handling and return the error as a string the model can react to, perhaps by trying a different query. Deduplicate URLs before synthesis and put timeouts on page fetches so one slow site doesn't hang the whole agent.

slides.title: Evaluating the Agent
bullets: Accuracy: do sources support the claims?
Coverage: were sub-questions addressed?
Citation quality: real, relevant URLs
Efficiency: iterations and cost
slides.narration: Finally, evaluate. Accuracy means each claim is actually supported by its cited source, so spot-check by opening URLs. Coverage asks whether the agent addressed the important sub-questions. Citation quality checks that links are real and relevant. And efficiency tracks how many iterations and how much money it took. Good citations matter as much as good prose.

slides.title: Recap & Next Steps
bullets: Agent = plan, act, observe, repeat, synthesize
Tools defined with JSON schemas
Structured, validated, cited output
Guardrails make it production-ready
slides.narration: To recap: you built an agent loop that plans, calls web tools, observes results, and synthesizes a structured report with citations, all wrapped in guardrails for safety and cost. Next, try adding more tools like a calculator or a PDF reader, and experiment with parallel sub-agents researching different angles simultaneously.
